references.text: The parallel passage in [ref:Matt 13:33|Matthew 13:33] presents the same parable about yeast that a woman hid in three measures of flour until it was all leavened. Luke and Matthew have almost identical wording.

[ref:Luk 13:18-20|Luke 13:18–20] provides the immediate context: Jesus asks what the kingdom of God is like, first tells the parable of the mustard seed, then introduces the yeast parable with "What shall I compare the kingdom of God to?"

In [ref:1 Kor 5:6-8|1 Corinthians 5:6–8], Paul uses the yeast metaphor but with opposite value: "A little yeast leavens the whole batch." Here he warns against the pervasive power of sin, while the parable in Luke speaks of the pervasive growth of God's kingdom.

In [ref:Gal 5:9|Galatians 5:9], Paul repeats the saying "A little yeast leavens the whole batch," again with a negative connotation—regarding false teaching—which highlights the power of the yeast image as a metaphor for something that permeates everything.

In [ref:1 Mos 18:6|Genesis 18:6], Abraham asks Sarah to take three seahs (measures) of fine flour and make cakes, the same amount (σάτα τρία) mentioned in the parable. The background from the patriarchal narrative may have given resonance to the image.

In [ref:2 Mos 12:15-20|Exodus 12:15–20], the laws concerning unleavened bread during the Passover celebration are given. Yeast (ζύμη) became a charged symbol in Jewish tradition through these regulations, which adds depth to Jesus' use of yeast as a positive image of God's kingdom.

In [ref:Matt 16:6-12|Matthew 16:6–12], Jesus warns against the yeast of the Pharisees and Sadducees, explaining that it is their teaching. This shows the flexibility of the yeast metaphor—it can be used both positively (as in Luke 13:21) and negatively.

In [ref:Luk 12:1|Luke 12:1], Jesus warns the disciples against the yeast of the Pharisees, which is hypocrisy. Thus, Luke uses the yeast image both negatively (here) and positively (in 13:21 regarding God's kingdom).
